title: Baizhang's Wild Fox

Whenever he ascended the hall, there was an old man who followed the assembly to hear the Dharma. One day, when the assembly withdrew, only the old man did not leave. The Master asked: “Who are you?” The old man said: “I am not a human being. In the time of the past Buddha Kashyapa, I once dwelt on this mountain. [Not deluded about cause and effect] With regard to karmic retribution
. A great practitioner is not muddled about karmic retribution
, and this does not mean that he does not receive karmic retribution

. Therefore Bodhisattvas fear the cause, and living beings fear the result. Because Bodhisattvas fear the cause, they dare not create evil causes; because living beings fear the result, they create evil causes recklessly under the drive of desire—and only when the evil retribution arrives do they feel terror and fear, but by then it is too late. A great practitioner understands karmic retribution: where there is a cause, there is bound to be a result. Therefore, when evil retribution appears before him, he does not give rise to thoughts of resentment, harm, or grief, and he does not create new evil karma. Only this is “not being deluded about cause and effect”: following conditions, he dissolves old karma and creates no fresh calamity. But ordinary people do not understand karmic retribution; when evil retribution appears, they blame heaven, earth, and others, but never blame themselves for having created the evil cause, and they are filled with anger, resentment, and a sense of grievance. This not only aggravates their suffering but may even lead them to create new evil karma. Karmic retribution is the fundamental law of the universe. As long as one is still within the dream of ignorance (regarding the dream of ignorance, see

), one will be subject to karmic retribution. The greatest confusion of people is confusion about karmic retribution, and hence there is the evil world of the five turbidities and the transmigration of the six realms. The greatest clarity is to understand karmic retribution (
not being deluded about cause and effect
), and this is the key to liberation.

Question: There is a saying: originally there is not a single thing, so what cause and effect can there be? Therefore the statement “a great practitioner does not fall into cause and effect” is also correct. Is this so?

Answer: “Originally there is not a single thing, so what cause and effect can there be”—this is said with reference to the true aspect of all phenomena. Yet within the true aspect of all phenomena there is neither cause and effect nor a great practitioner, so where does one begin to speak of “whether a great practitioner falls into cause and effect”? Therefore the statement “a great practitioner does not fall into cause and effect” is made with reference to the phenomena within the dream of ignorance. Within the dream of ignorance, cause and effect is a fundamental law as hard as iron, and the statement “a great practitioner does not fall into cause and effect” is utterly wrong! Hence he fell into the body of a wild fox.

In commentaries on Chan koans, one often finds the perfectly still no-thingness of the true aspect of all phenomena mixed together with the multifarious phenomena of the dream of ignorance—obscure mystification and idle tangling of words. When reading, one should pay a little attention and not be led astray by them.
